ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Acute compartment syndrome: 3

An unconscious trauma patient has a swollen limb and cannot report pain or cooperate with examination. The team suspects compartment syndrome but the clinical assessment is unreliable. Which adjunct can help evaluate the pressure-related risk?

  1. Preserved pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome
  2. Urgent surgical decompression
  3. Ischemic muscle contracture
  4. Compartment-pressure assessment when needed
  5. Acute compartment syndrome
Answer and explanation

Compartment-pressure assessment when needed

Pressure measurement can support diagnosis when the examination is unreliable; it must not delay obvious emergency treatment.

Option explanations

Compartment-pressure assessment when needed: Pressure measurement can support diagnosis when the examination is unreliable; it must not delay obvious emergency treatment.

Acute compartment syndrome: Escalating pain, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment after injury are concerning for pressure-related ischemia. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Preserved pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome: Major arterial flow can remain present while microvascular tissue perfusion is compromised. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Urgent surgical decompression: Established acute compartment syndrome requires urgent specialist treatment, usually fasciotomy. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Ischemic muscle contracture: Untreated ischemia can cause muscle necrosis, fibrosis and permanent contracture. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
